title: Spherical Menelaus Theorem via Sin Measure Function
description: Formalizes the spherical Menelaus theorem — the great-circle transversal analogue of the spherical Ceva theorem. Uses sin as the measure function for signed geodesic arcs, exactly paralleling the hyperbolic case (OQ02) which uses sinh. Proves the complete 2×2 matrix: Ceva/Menelaus × Euclidean/Spherical/Hyperbolic.

overview.historicalContext:
Menelaus of Alexandria (c. 70-140 CE) first stated his transversal theorem in the 'Sphaerica', a treatise on spherical geometry — ironically, the spherical version came first! The Euclidean version was later derived as a limiting case. The theorem characterizes when three points D (on BC), E (on CA), F (on AB) are collinear: the product of signed ratios equals -1.

On the sphere, straight lines become great circles, and lengths become arcs. The spherical Menelaus theorem replaces the Euclidean ratio BD/DC with sin(BD)/sin(DC), where BD is a signed arc length. This substitution works because sin is an odd function — sin(-x) = -sin(x) — exactly preserving the sign convention for directed arcs.

The spherical case has a subtlety absent from both Euclidean and hyperbolic versions: sin is periodic and zero at multiples of π, so domain restrictions are needed (arcs must avoid kπ). For arcs in (0, π) — which corresponds to geodesic segments strictly between vertices — sin is strictly positive. The signed-arc framework handles arcs in (-π, 0) (exterior direction) using sin's odd symmetry.

This formalization completes the 2×2 matrix: the parent file (CevasTheoremNonEuclidean.lean) proved spherical Ceva; OQ02 proved hyperbolic Menelaus; this file proves spherical Menelaus. The algebraic core is identical across all three geometries — only the measure function changes.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize the spherical analogue of Menelaus' theorem: for a geodesic triangle $ABC$ on a sphere, if a great circle (transversal) meets lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at points $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively, then $D$, $E$, $F$ are collinear (on a great circle) if and only if $\frac{\sin(BD)}{\sin(DC)} \cdot \frac{\sin(CE)}{\sin(EA)} \cdot \frac{\sin(AF)}{\sin(FB)} = -1$ where arcs are signed (positive = internal division, negative = external).
overview.proofStrategy: The proof reduces to a single algebraic lemma `menelaus_algebraic_core`: the product of three ratios equals -1 iff the numerator product equals the negative of the denominator product. This is proved via `div_mul_div_comm` and `div_eq_iff`. The spherical Menelaus theorem is then a 2-line consequence: unfold the definition and apply the core lemma. The key technical steps are: (1) proving sin x ≠ 0 for arcs in (0,π) via `Real.sin_pos_of_pos_of_lt_pi`, (2) handling exterior arcs via sin's odd symmetry `Real.sin_neg`.
keyInsights: The algebraic core (product = -1 iff numerator = -denominator) is geometry-independent: the same proof works for Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic Menelaus theorems
sin and sinh are both odd functions, so both naturally encode signed arcs/distances — sin(-x) = -sin(x) for arcs, sinh(-x) = -sinh(x) for distances
The domain restriction for spherical geometry (sin ≠ 0, i.e., arcs ≠ kπ) has no hyperbolic analogue since sinh is globally nonzero away from 0
When all arcs are interior (in (0,π)), the product is strictly positive and hence can never equal -1 — a geometric sanity check proved formally
The 2×2 matrix (Ceva/Menelaus × Euclidean/Spherical/Hyperbolic) is now complete in this gallery, all following the same algebraic pattern
prerequisites: Spherical trigonometry and great circle arcs
Hyperbolic Menelaus (OQ02 sibling) for the sinh analogy

sections.title: sin Properties for Signed Arcs
sections.summary: Proves that sin is positive on (0,π), nonzero on (0,π) and (-π,0), and satisfies sin(-x) = -sin(x). These justify the signed-arc framework: non-degeneracy conditions are automatic for arcs in these intervals.
sections.mathContext: For geodesic triangle sides, arcs naturally lie in $(0,\pi)$. For exterior division points, arcs lie in $(-\pi, 0)$. sin is nonzero on both intervals, enabling well-defined ratios $\sin(BD)/\sin(DC)$.

sections.title: Algebraic Core: Menelaus Ratio Product
sections.summary: Defines menelausRatioProduct (a/b)·(c/d)·(e/f) and proves the fundamental biconditional: this product equals -1 iff a·c·e = -(b·d·f). This is the heart of the proof, shared by all three geometries.
sections.mathContext: Key tactic: `rw [div_mul_div_comm, div_mul_div_comm]` reduces to a single fraction, then `div_eq_iff` converts to a ring equality, solved by `linarith`.

sections.title: SphericalMenelausConfig Structure
sections.summary: Defines the SphericalMenelausConfig structure with six signed arcs and three non-degeneracy hypotheses (sin ≠ 0 for the denominator arcs). Also defines sphericalMenelausProduct as a specialization of menelausRatioProduct.
sections.mathContext: The non-degeneracy constraints are `Real.sin dc ≠ 0` etc., rather than `dc ≠ 0` as in the hyperbolic case. This reflects that sin has zeros at multiples of π, not just at 0.

sections.title: Spherical Menelaus Theorem
sections.summary: The main theorem: sphericalMenelausProduct cfg = -1 iff the sin cross-product condition holds. Proved in 2 lines by applying menelaus_algebraic_core.

sections.title: Interior-Arc Specialization
sections.summary: Proves that when all six arcs lie in (0,π), the Menelaus product is strictly positive and hence cannot equal -1. This confirms the geometric content: at least one division point must be external for collinearity.
sections.mathContext: Geometric fact: a transversal to a triangle must cross an odd number of sides externally. All-interior configurations give a positive product, not -1.

sections.title: Ceva-Menelaus Duality and Examples
sections.summary: Proves the algebraic duality between spherical Ceva (product = 1) and spherical Menelaus (product = -1). Also provides a midpoint example (when BD = DC, the first ratio is 1) and a comparison with the Euclidean case (direct lengths vs sin).
sections.mathContext: Ceva: $P = 1 \iff \sin(BD)\sin(CE)\sin(AF) = \sin(DC)\sin(EA)\sin(FB)$. Menelaus: $P = -1 \iff$ same with negation. Both are proved by `menelaus_algebraic_core` with appropriate target.

conclusion.summary: This formalization proves the spherical Menelaus theorem with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. The proof is a 2-line consequence of a reusable algebraic core, demonstrating that all three geometries (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) share identical algebraic structure — only the measure function changes.
conclusion.implications: The completion of the 2×2 matrix (Ceva/Menelaus × Euclidean/Spherical/Hyperbolic) suggests a natural next question: is there a unified statement parametrized by the measure function? The pattern f(-x) = -f(x) (odd function) is the key property, suggesting the real claim is: for any odd function f with f(x) ≠ 0 in the relevant domain, the f-Menelaus theorem holds with the same algebraic core.
openQuestions: Is there a unified Menelaus theorem parametrized by an odd function f? The algebraic core `menelaus_algebraic_core` already proves this — the remaining work is to characterize the appropriate domains for each geometry.
Is there a unified Ceva-Menelaus duality that captures both as special cases of a single theorem about cross-ratios in projective space?
